title: How force opens a channel
objective: Explain how mechanically gated channels convert membrane force into current.

steps.title: Sensing touch is a physics problem
steps.body:
Light, heat and chemicals carry energy a channel can catch. Force is harder: a touch neuron has to turn a *mechanical* push into an ionic current in under a millisecond.

The answer is **[[mechanically activated channel|mechanically activated channels]]**: ion channels that open when the membrane around them is stretched or deformed.

steps.title: Force-from-lipid, force-from-filament
steps.body:
Two broad ideas for how force reaches the channel:

- **Force-from-lipid:** tension in the membrane itself bends the channel open. [[Piezo2]] works largely this way.
- **Force-from-filament:** the channel is tethered to the cytoskeleton or matrix, and movement pulls it open.

Either way, the gate responds to mechanical stress, not voltage or a ligand.

flag.note: Real endings may combine both mechanisms; details are still being worked out.

visual.alt: A push creates tension in the membrane, which bends a Piezo channel open; cations then flow from outside into the cell.
visual.caption: Membrane tension bends the channel open — force becomes current directly.

options: The channel is opened directly by force, with no second-messenger relay in between
It uses a slow enzyme cascade
It waits for calcium from stores
steps.explanation: Directly mechanically gated channels skip the slow biochemical relays, so touch can be signaled almost instantly, fast enough to adjust grip in real time.

steps.setup: You stretch a patch of membrane containing a mechanically activated channel in a dish, with no other cells around.
options: No, it needs a whole animal
Yes: if the channel is intrinsically mechanosensitive, membrane tension alone can open it
steps.reveal: A channel that opens to membrane stretch in an isolated patch is intrinsically mechanosensitive. That experiment is exactly how Piezo channels were pinned down (next lesson).
